text:
Keep the Join: The Case for Teaching Joined-Up Handwriting

Every few years someone proposes that primary schools stop teaching joined-up handwriting. The argument is tidy. Children will type for the rest of their lives, so why spend precious hours teaching them to loop an e into an l? Finland moved in that direction in 2016, dropping compulsory cursive in favour of print and keyboard skills, and educators elsewhere have watched with interest. I think they should not follow. Primary schools should keep teaching joined-up handwriting, and teach it properly. The reasons are practical, cognitive and, in the end, about fairness.

Start with the claim that handwriting is obsolete. It is not. Pupils still write by hand in most classrooms, in exercise books, on worksheets and in exams. In England, national tests and GCSEs are still sat with pen and paper. A child who cannot write quickly and legibly is working under a handicap in every one of those settings. The real question is not whether children will handwrite but how well. A fluent hand is a tool that frees attention. A laboured one eats it.

That is the heart of the first argument, which is fluency. Print letters make the pen lift after almost every stroke, and each lift is a small decision about where to land next. Joined writing removes many of those decisions. The pen stays on the page and the movement becomes rhythmic, almost automatic. Studies of handwriting speed are mixed, and it would be dishonest to claim that joined script is always faster. But the better evidence suggests that children with a well-practised joined style write faster and with less effort than those who print, once the habit is secure. A child who writes automatically has working memory left over for the thing that matters, which is what to say. Research on writing development has long found that transcription skills, meaning handwriting and spelling, constrain the quality of children's composition. When the hand is slow, ideas get dropped on the way to the page.

The second argument concerns spelling. Joining letters turns a word into a single movement. Teachers who introduce joins early report that children absorb common letter strings such as ing, ight and tion as physical patterns. The hand remembers what the eye might miss. This is not magic and I would not overstate it, but it fits what we know about how motor memory supports learning. Printing a word is a series of separate acts. Joining it is one gesture with a shape, and shapes are easier to recall than lists.

Third, there is the evidence from neuroscience. Brain imaging studies, including work from Norway and the United States, have found that writing by hand activates wider networks than keyboarding, particularly regions tied to learning and memory. Some of this work looks at cursive specifically and some at handwriting in general, so we should be careful about what it shows. It does not prove that joined writing beats print. It does show that the physical formation of letters does something for the developing brain that tapping keys does not. A school that abandons handwriting entirely takes a risk with that. A school that keeps handwriting, and chooses the joined form because it is the most efficient version, is on safer ground.

Fourth, and rarely mentioned in these debates, is dyslexia. Many specialists favour joined writing for children who struggle with letter orientation, because it helps prevent reversals. In print, b, d, p and q are the same shape turned or flipped, which is exactly what trips up a child who finds orientation hard. A joined script with entry strokes gives each letter its own path from the baseline. This is not true for every child, and some do better with print, but it is a reason to teach the join, not to drop it.

Now to the strongest objection, which is opportunity cost. Primary timetables are crowded, and every minute spent on loops and joins is a minute not spent on reading, number or science. I take this seriously, but the cost is smaller than critics suggest. Handwriting does not need long lessons. Ten minutes a day, taught well, is enough for most children to reach fluency by the end of the junior years, and the practice can be folded into the writing they are already doing. The real waste is the opposite approach, in which schools teach print in the early years, then expect children to develop a joined style on their own, or teach joins so late and so briefly that pupils invent inefficient hybrids. A deliberate, early, consistent programme is cheaper than the muddle that follows a half-hearted one.

The second objection is that typing is the future. In part it is. Children should learn to type, and primary school is the right place, from about the age of eight or nine when their hands are ready. But this is not a choice between two skills. Nobody argues that learning to type should replace learning to draw, or that calculators should replace mental arithmetic. We teach foundations by hand because the doing builds the understanding. Handwriting and keyboarding serve different purposes. One suits notes, exams, quick drafts and private thought, the other polished and shared text. A well-educated adult needs both. Studies of university students suggest that those who take notes by hand often process lectures more deeply than those who transcribe on laptops, because the slowness forces them to summarise. A hand that can keep up, and do so fluently, is an asset there too.

A third objection holds that joined writing is elitist, a relic of copperplate and penmanship prizes. The reverse is closer to the truth. The children who suffer most from poor handwriting teaching are those whose homes offer no extra practice and no tutors. Wealthier families will make sure their children write neatly whatever the school does, because they can buy the time and support. If schools stop teaching joined writing, the skill does not vanish. It becomes a private advantage, passed to those whose parents think to provide it. Meanwhile examiners and teachers still read scripts, and untidy handwriting is penalised, consciously or not. Studies have found that neat scripts receive higher marks than identical content written messily. Teaching a clear, fluent hand to every child is a modest form of levelling up, and it costs very little.

What would good teaching look like? It would begin in reception with print-style letter formation that uses entry and exit strokes from the start, so that the later step to joining is natural rather than a fresh learning task. It would introduce joins in the second year, gradually, beginning with the easiest and most common, and build through short daily practice. It would pay attention to posture, pencil grip and paper position, which matter more than most adults realise. And it would be assessed lightly, with feedback aimed at legibility and fluency rather than beauty. No child should be marked down for failing to produce a perfect looped f. The goal is a personal, readable, speedy hand, not a calligrapher's.

It would also leave room for flexibility. By the upper juniors many children develop a style that mixes joined and unjoined letters, and fast, legible writers often do exactly this. The aim of teaching joins is not rigid uniformity but giving children a base from which to build their own efficient script. Without a starting point, pupils improvise, and improvisation under exam pressure produces the illegible scrawl that secondary teachers complain about.

I should concede what the evidence does not show. No study demonstrates that joined writing makes a child cleverer, and the claims sometimes made on its behalf about intelligence or character are nonsense. The research on speed is mixed. Some children genuinely write better in print and should be allowed to. Teaching joined-up handwriting is not a crusade. It is a modest, practical judgment. Children will write by hand for years, fluency frees the mind, and joining offers real if moderate advantages in speed, spelling and legibility for many learners. So schools should teach it as the default and permit sensible exceptions.

The alternative rests on a prediction that handwriting will fade away. That prediction has been made for decades and keeps failing, because pen and paper remain the cheapest, most reliable and most private technology a child can use. They need no battery and no login, and they send no notifications. In an age when so much of childhood happens on screens, a quiet physical skill taught at school seems worth defending rather than dismantling.

So keep the join. Teach it early, briefly and well, and treat it as one tool among several, valued for what it does rather than for nostalgia. The child who leaves primary school with a fast, legible hand has gained something that will serve them in every exam hall, every set of notes and every card written, for the rest of their life. That is a good return on ten minutes a day.
